claim: Median monthly Patreon earnings for creators affiliated with a single major platform sit between $42 and $77 per month across all platforms and years 2018-2024, even after excluding everyone earning under $10/month.
stance_target: The typical content creator earns nowhere near a living wage from platform monetization
scope_conditions: Patreon administrative earnings data only (one revenue stream, not total creator income); creators with exactly one external platform affiliation; sample floored at >$10/month so the true median across all Patreon accounts is lower; geography not reported, Patreon creator base is US/Western-skewed
region: Not stated; Patreon is a US platform with a Western-skewed creator base, earnings in USD

claim: Mean creator earnings exceed median creator earnings by a factor of roughly 4 to 6 on every platform studied, so any figure reported as an 'average creator income' overstates the typical creator's earnings several-fold.
stance_target: Mean-based creator income statistics are systematically misleading
scope_conditions: Patreon monthly earnings, pooled 2018/2021/2024, creators >$10/month with single-platform affiliation

claim: Creator earnings follow a Pareto power law with exponent alpha of approximately 2.0, placing them closer to concentrated capital income (alpha ~1.5) than to labour income.
stance_target: Content creation behaves as a superstar/winner-take-all market rather than a normal occupation
scope_conditions: Clauset-Newman-Shalizi MLE power-law fit on Patreon monthly earnings; cross-sectional, no causal identification
quoted_support: Our core finding is that monthly Patreon earnings across platforms fit a power law with exponent around α ≈2.0, indicating an extremely heavy-tailed distribution and a strong "rich-get-richer" dynamic.
numbers: 2024: YouTube 1.80, Instagram 1.84, Twitch 1.93, Facebook 1.94, Patreon 2.24, Twitter/X 2.35

claim: The winner-take-all regime in creator earnings begins at only $26-$70 per month, versus conventional national income distributions where the Pareto tail only applies above roughly $100,000 per year.
stance_target: Creator income concentration is qualitatively unlike ordinary labour markets and affects the whole distribution, not just the top
scope_conditions: Patreon monthly earnings 2018-2024; comparison income-distribution figure drawn from Dragulescu & Yakovenko 2001 and Tao et al. 2019
quoted_support: Power law dynamics emerge early at between $26 and $70 per monthly earnings across these platforms, a very low monthly earnings amount consistent across platforms. At an annual amount of $312 to $840, this is in stark contrast to standard income distributions, where the power law typically applies to income levels only above $100,000 per annum
numbers: $100,000 per annum threshold for conventional incomes

claim: Earnings concentration among creators worsened over time on YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and Twitch between 2018 and 2024, with the Pareto exponent falling on each.
stance_target: Conditions for mid-tier creators have deteriorated rather than improved as the creator economy matured
scope_conditions: Only three cross-sections (2018, 2021, 2024); authors caution some platform-year estimates are sensitive to estimator choice; compositional change in the creator population is an unruled-out alternative explanation
quoted_support: Instagram's α dropped from around 2.1 in 2021 to around 1.84 in 2024, a period that coincided with the platform's shift toward algorithmic recommendation.

claim: Platforms whose earnings are more concentrated also have LOWER median and mean earnings, meaning concentration does not simply redistribute a fixed pot upward but is associated with a smaller middle tier overall.
stance_target: Algorithmic concentration erodes the creator middle class
scope_conditions: Cross-platform correlation across six platforms, Patreon earnings only; correlational not causal
quoted_support: Figure 3 shows a clear association between the power law exponent (α) and the median of the earnings distribution: platforms with higher median earnings tend to exhibit less heavy-tailed distributions (higher α).
numbers: median range $40-$65 on the plotted axis

claim: With a Pareto exponent near 2, a tenfold increase in creator earnings makes creators at that level roughly ten times rarer, implying that for every 10,000 creators earning $100 only about 1 earns $1,000,000.
stance_target: The odds of reaching high creator income are quantifiably remote
scope_conditions: Analytic implication of the fitted alpha ~ 2, applied to Patreon monthly earnings; illustrative rather than a direct count
quoted_support: For example, if 10,000 creators earn at least $100, we would expect around 1,000 to earn at least $1,000, about 100 to earn at least $10,000, and roughly 1 to earn at least $1,000,000.

claim: Patreon crowdfunding links appear in only 2.55% of YouTube video descriptions versus 49% for cross-platform links, so Patreon-based earnings measures capture a small and selected slice of total creator income.
stance_target: Scope limits on using Patreon data as a proxy for total creator earnings
scope_conditions: Cited by the authors as a footnote from a separate study of YouTube video descriptions
quoted_support: One study finds 2.55% of YouTube video descriptions contain crowdfunding links versus 49% for cross-platform links.

claim: Platforms do not disclose creator earnings or algorithmic optimizations, and social media platforms are not covered by national statistical classifications such as the US Census Bureau, which is why systematic creator-income evidence is nearly absent.
stance_target: There is a documented data vacuum on creator occupational statistics
scope_conditions: Authors' framing of the literature gap as of July 2026
quoted_support: Unfortunately, there is little detailed evidence of the economic impact of algorithmic attention mechanisms, since platforms do not disclose creator earnings or algorithmic optimizations

claim: The share of Twitter/X-affiliated Patreon creators producing NSFW content rose from 45% in 2018 to 58% in 2024, which the authors flag as a compositional confound for that platform's more equal earnings distribution.
stance_target: Cross-platform differences in earnings inequality are driven purely by algorithm design
scope_conditions: Patreon creators whose only external platform is Twitter/X
quoted_support: ‘NSFW’ (not safe for work) creators increased on the platform by almost 30 percentage points, going from 45% and 46% of Patreon creators on Twitter/X in 2018 and 2021, respectively, to 58% in 2024
